AC9M10A05.title: Functions, Relations and Digital Conjectures
AC9M10A05.meaning: Explore functions and relations with digital tools, test conjectures against evidence and counterexamples, and generalise patterns carefully.
AC9M10A05.prereq: You should be comfortable plotting coordinates, reading graphs, substituting into formulas, recognising linear, quadratic and exponential relations, and solving simple equations. You should also know that an intersection point satisfies both relations.
AC9M10A05.reason: A student claims that increasing a in y=a(x-2)²+1 always moves the vertex upward. Design a digital investigation that tests the claim, include at least four values of a (positive, negative and zero), and write the strongest conclusion justified by your evidence.
AC9M10A05.teacher: Ask students to predict before using a graphing tool, then require a written evidence table and a counterexample search. Assess the quality of the generalisation, not the attractiveness of the graph.
AC9M10A05.parent: Ask your child to explain what they changed, what stayed fixed, and what evidence would prove their idea wrong. This turns digital graphing from button-pressing into mathematical reasoning.
hints: vary one parameter at a time
record the graph window or numerical interval used
AC9M10A05.vic: VC2M10A11, A16; VC2M10AA10 extends — Level 10/10A Algebra
AC9M10A05.nsw: Stage 5 Path Functions and graphs; Working mathematically

AC9M10M01.title: Composite Surface Area and Volume
AC9M10M01.meaning: Solve surface-area and volume problems for composite objects by decomposing solids, managing joined faces and using appropriate units.
AC9M10M01.prereq: Revise areas of rectangles and circles, volume of prisms and cylinders, metric conversions, π, and the difference between square and cubic units.
AC9M10M01.reason: A community event needs storage for 240 containers, each modelled as a 12 cm × 8 cm × 6 cm rectangular prism. Compare the theoretical packed volume with a freezer offering 1.6 m³ usable space. Then explain why volume alone may not guarantee the containers fit.
AC9M10M01.teacher: Use physical boxes or quick sketches to make joined faces visible. Ask students to annotate every exposed face before writing any surface-area formula; this prevents the most common error.
AC9M10M01.parent: Ask your child to point to the parts they are adding or subtracting and to explain whether the answer should be in square or cubic units before they calculate.
hints: for surface area, mark exposed faces only
convert all lengths to one unit first
keep π until the final rounding step
AC9M10M01.nsw: Stage 5 Core Length, area and volume; Path Further area and volume

AC9M10M02.title: Logarithmic Scales and Orders of Magnitude
AC9M10M02.meaning: Interpret logarithmic scales in contexts with very small, very large or multiplicatively changing quantities.
AC9M10M02.prereq: You should understand powers of 10, scientific notation, ratios, graph axes and exponential growth. Formal logarithm laws are not required for the core lesson.
AC9M10M02.reason: A dataset contains values 8×10¹, 3×10³, 7×10⁵ and 2×10⁸. Design a suitable axis for a graph, explain why you chose it, and describe what information a reader might misinterpret if the axis type were not labelled.
AC9M10M02.teacher: Use side-by-side linear and log plots of the same wide-ranging dataset. Ask students to write what each display makes easier or harder to see rather than presenting log scale as universally superior.
AC9M10M02.parent: Have your child explain why 10, 100 and 1000 can be equally spaced even though the ordinary differences are not equal. That explanation reveals whether the core idea is secure.
hints: compare exponents for orders of magnitude
linear = equal differences; log = equal ratios
AC9M10M02.nsw: Stage 5 supporting links across Number and finance and Functions and graphs

AC9M10M03.title: Right-Triangle Trigonometry, Bearings and Elevation
AC9M10M03.meaning: Use Pythagoras and right-triangle trigonometry to solve practical direction, bearing, elevation and depression problems.
AC9M10M03.prereq: Revise right triangles, Pythagoras’ theorem, angle properties, scale diagrams, calculator degree mode, rearranging simple equations and the SOH–CAH–TOA ratios.
AC9M10M03.reason: Two surveyors estimate a building height. One stands 40 m from the base and measures an elevation angle of 52° from eye height 1.6 m. The other stands 65 m away and measures 38°. Calculate both estimates and discuss what measurement or modelling issues could explain any difference.
AC9M10M03.teacher: Require a labelled diagram and ratio statement before calculator use. Include problems where Pythagoras is the better choice so students learn selection, not just formula matching.
AC9M10M03.parent: Ask your child to explain why they chose sine, cosine or tangent before calculating. If they can identify opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse correctly, most routine errors disappear.
hints: label O/A/H relative to the chosen angle
bearings start at north and turn clockwise
AC9M10M03.nsw: Stage 5 Core Pythagoras and trigonometry; Path Further trigonometry

AC9M10M04.title: Measurement Error and Accuracy
AC9M10M04.meaning: Identify how measurement uncertainty and error affect calculated results, decisions and reported accuracy.
AC9M10M04.prereq: Revise rounding, significant figures, percentage change, unit conversion and formulas involving measured lengths, areas, volumes and rates.
AC9M10M04.reason: A manufacturer accepts rods between 499.5 mm and 500.5 mm. A measuring device has a possible systematic offset of +0.4 mm and random variation of ±0.2 mm. Explain how a displayed 500.0 mm reading could lead to an incorrect accept/reject decision and propose a better checking procedure.
AC9M10M04.teacher: Use practical measurement stations with rulers, scales and timing tasks. Ask students to predict whether repetition or calibration would improve each situation, then justify the answer.
AC9M10M04.parent: Use everyday examples such as kitchen scales, tape measures or fuel gauges. Ask whether the measurement needs to be exact enough for the decision being made.
hints: check whether calculations square/cube/repeat the measured quantity
judge impact against the decision tolerance
AC9M10M04.vic: VC2M10M04 — Level 10 Measurement (measurement error within modelling)
AC9M10M04.nsw: Stage 5 measurement/space contexts with Working mathematically

AC9M10M05.title: Proportion, Scale and Mathematical Modelling
AC9M10M05.meaning: Model practical situations involving proportion and scale, including how lengths, areas and volumes change under scaling.
AC9M10M05.prereq: Revise ratios, unit conversion, similar shapes, percentages, area and volume formulas, and solving simple proportional equations.
AC9M10M05.reason: A company wants a display model of a 24 m × 10 m × 8 m building to fit inside a 1.2 m-long case. Choose a suitable uniform scale, calculate model dimensions, estimate the volume scale factor, and discuss at least two practical features that the simple geometric model ignores.
AC9M10M05.teacher: Move beyond scale worksheets into design decisions. Require students to include an assumptions box and a short model-evaluation paragraph with every substantial task.
AC9M10M05.parent: Ask your child what changes when a model is doubled in every dimension. If they say area ×4 and volume ×8 and can explain why, the key scaling idea is secure.
hints: linear k → area k² → volume k³
state assumptions before trusting the result
AC9M10M05.nsw: Stage 5 Core Ratios and rates; Path Variation and rates of change

AC9M10SP01.title: Deductive Geometry and Proof
AC9M10SP01.meaning: Use definitions, angle facts and geometric theorems in deductive proofs and spatial problem solving.
AC9M10SP01.prereq: Revise angle sums, parallel-line angle relationships, triangle properties, congruence tests, similarity, scale factors and basic algebra.
AC9M10SP01.reason: Write a complete proof that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal by constructing a line from the vertex to the midpoint of the base. Your proof must identify two congruent triangles and justify the congruence test before using corresponding angles.
AC9M10SP01.teacher: Mark reasons as strictly as numerical answers. Include deliberately misleading diagrams so students learn that visual appearance is not evidence.
AC9M10SP01.parent: Ask your child 'How do you know?' after every geometric statement. A complete answer should name a theorem or fact rather than say the diagram looks that way.
hints: use one justified step at a time
AC9M10SP01.nsw: Stage 5 Core Geometrical properties and figures; Path Geometrical figures and proof

AC9M10SP02.title: Networks, Paths and Connectedness
AC9M10SP02.meaning: Interpret networks as vertices and edges, analyse connectedness and use network diagrams in practical situations.
AC9M10SP02.prereq: You need basic graph-reading skills, logical reasoning and comfort following multi-step routes. No advanced graph theory is assumed.
AC9M10SP02.reason: Model a small school-bus network with at least six stops. Define vertices and edges, identify the degree of each stop, decide whether the network is connected, and explain one vulnerability if a road link becomes unavailable.
AC9M10SP02.teacher: Use transport and dependency examples where visual distance is deliberately misleading. Ask students to state the network definition before answering route questions.
AC9M10SP02.parent: Use a train map or family of connected devices. Ask what the dots and lines mean and whether every point can reach every other point.
hints: do not infer physical distance from drawing position
